title: Memory Requirements Estimation
description: Estimate RAM needs for application servers, databases, and caches to avoid swapping and latency spikes.

data.text: Memory is one of the fastest and most expensive resources in your system. Estimating memory requirements prevents swapping, reduces latency, and keeps your application responsive under load.

Application servers need memory for the runtime, loaded libraries, request objects, and in-memory caches. Measure heap usage with profiling tools under realistic load, then add a 30-50% safety buffer.
Baseline is about 190 MB. At 1,000 concurrent requests, add 500 MB. Total = ~700 MB per server. With a 4 GB instance, you can run roughly 5 API servers comfortably.

Databases use memory for buffer pools, query caches, and connection handling. PostgreSQL recommends allocating 25% of server memory to the shared buffer pool, while MySQL InnoDB often benefits from 50-70% for the buffer pool on dedicated database servers.

data.title: The 80/20 Rule
data.text: Keeping 80% of hot data in memory reduces disk I/O significantly. If your working set is 100 GB, plan for at least 100 GB of RAM on your primary database.
For a 500 GB dataset with 20% hot data (100 GB), a database server needs at least 100 GB RAM for the buffer pool, plus 20 GB for OS and background processes. Total = ~128 GB.
Caches store frequently accessed data in memory. Estimate cache memory by multiplying the number of cached objects by their average size, then add overhead for metadata, indexing, and fragmentation.
A Redis cluster with 4 GB RAM can comfortably hold this cache with room for growth. Redis uses about 1.5x the raw data size due to overhead, so always multiply your data estimate by 1.5.

terms.definition: An in-memory cache of database pages that reduces disk I/O.
The subset of data actively used by the application, typically 10-30% of total data.
When the OS moves memory pages to disk because RAM is exhausted, causing severe performance degradation.

data.title: Memory Estimation Rules
points: Profile application memory under realistic load
Allocate 25-70% of DB memory to buffer pools
Cache size = data size x 1.5 for Redis overhead
Keep 80% of hot data in memory
data.takeaway: Memory estimation prevents swapping and keeps latency low.

data.title: Practice Calculation
data.description: A PostgreSQL database holds 200 GB of user data with 15% hot data. Estimate the RAM needed for the primary database server.
data.expectedOutcome: Hot data = ~30 GB; plan for 30 GB buffer pool + 8 GB overhead = 40 GB minimum

items.question: What is the cost of underestimating memory?
items.answer: The OS starts swapping pages to disk, increasing latency from microseconds to milliseconds. This causes cascading performance issues across the entire system.

items.question: Should I use swap space on production servers?
items.answer: Yes, as a safety net, but rely on it sparingly. Monitor swap usage and treat sustained swapping as an emergency signal.
